title: Audio Lesson: Delegation Patterns
limitations: Generated from concept pages; not yet reviewed.
Content may drift from source; verify against current main.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A single agent working alone hits a ceiling. It can't review its own work objectively, it can't parallelize, and it can't specialize. Multi-agent delegation solves this with three patterns, each with different trade-offs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Coordinator pattern gives each worker a self-contained specification with zero context inheritance. The coordinator digests findings into precise instructions. This is the safest pattern — no context leakage between workers — but the slowest because the coordinator must synthesize everything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Fork pattern copies the full parent context into a child. It's fast for quick exploration but restricted to single-level — a forked child cannot fork again. This recursive fork guard prevents context explosion.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Swarm pattern uses a shared task queue. Peers register, claim tasks, and post results. No peer can spawn new peers — it's a flat roster. This works well for batch processing where many independent tasks need parallel execution.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Each worker gets filtered tools. Researchers get read-only access. Implementers get specific write tools. Verifiers get no tools at all — they analyze, they don't act. This principle of least privilege prevents accidents.
